items.stem:
Given the R program
  f = function (n) { x = 1; for (i in 1:n) { x = x * i }; x }
  f(4)
which of the following is the output?
items.explanation: Trace the loop: the loop multiplies x by 1, 2, 3, 4, so f(4) = 4! = 24; 10 would be the sum. Trap: check exactly when the loop stops and what is accumulated. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:
Given the R program
  f = function (n) { s = 0; for (i in 1:n) { s = s + i^2 }; s }
  f(3)
which of the following is the output?
items.explanation: Trace the loop: s accumulates 1² + 2² + 3² = 14; 6 is 1 + 2 + 3 and 36 is (1 + 2 + 3)². Trap: check exactly when the loop stops and what is accumulated. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:
Given the R program

  f(5)
which of the following is the output?
items.explanation: Trace the loop: 2 is added five times, so x = 10; 32 would be 2⁵. Trap: check exactly when the loop stops and what is accumulated. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:
Given the R program
  f = function (n) { x = 1; while (x < n) { x = x * 2 }; x }
  f(20)
which of the following is the output?
items.explanation: Trace the loop: x doubles 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and stops as soon as x < 20 fails, i.e. at 32; 16 is the last value that was still below 20. Trap: check exactly when the loop stops and what is accumulated. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:
Given the R program
  f = function (v) { s = 0; for (e in v) { if (e > 0) s = s + e }; s }
  f(c(3, −1, 4, −5, 2))
which of the following is the output?
items.explanation: Trace the loop: only the positive elements 3, 4 and 2 are added, giving 9; the plain sum would be 3. Trap: check exactly when the loop stops and what is accumulated. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:
Given the R program
  f = function (n) { x = 0; for (i in 1:n) { for (j in 1:i) { x = x + 1 } }; x }
  f(4)
which of the following is the output?
items.explanation: Trace the loop: the inner loop runs i times, so x = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10; 16 would be 4 × 4. Trap: check exactly when the loop stops and what is accumulated. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:
Given the R program
  f = function (n) { x = 1; for (i in seq(1, n, by = 2)) { x = x * i }; x }
  f(7)
which of the following is the output?
items.explanation: Trace the loop: seq(1, 7, by = 2) is 1, 3, 5, 7, whose product is 105; 5040 is 7!. Trap: check exactly when the loop stops and what is accumulated. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:

which of the following is the output?
items.explanation: Trace the loop: v grows to (1, 4, 9, 16) and its sum is 30; 16 is only the last element. Trap: check exactly when the loop stops and what is accumulated. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

  f(4)
which of the following is the output?
items.explanation: Trace the loop: 10 − 1 − 2 − 3 − 4 = 0; 6 would subtract only 4. Trap: check exactly when the loop stops and what is accumulated. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem:
Given the R program
  f = function (n) { k = 0; repeat { k = k + 1; if (k^2 > n) break }; k }
  f(30)
which of the following is the output?
items.explanation: Trace the loop: the loop stops at the first k with k² > 30, which is k = 6 (36 > 30); 5 is the last k with k² ≤ 30. Trap: check exactly when the loop stops and what is accumulated. (Output confirmed by running the code in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem: With x <- c(5, −2, 8, −7, 0), match LIST-I with LIST-II. LIST-I: A. > min(x); B. > max(x); C. > range(x); D. > which(x < 0). LIST-II: I. [1] 8; II. [1] −7; III. [1] 2 4; IV. [1] −7  8. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: min and max return single values, range returns both extremes as a pair, and which returns the positions (indices) where its logical condition is TRUE, not the values: min(x) gives [1] −7; max(x) gives [1] 8; range(x) gives [1] −7  8; which(x < 0) gives [1] 2 4. So the matching is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III. Trap: which() gives indices; and it needs a logical argument such as x < 0. (Outputs confirmed in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem: With x <- c(3, 10, −1, 6), match LIST-I with LIST-II. LIST-I: A. > min(x); B. > max(x); C. > range(x); D. > which(x > 5). LIST-II: I. [1] −1 10; II. [1] 10; III. [1] −1; IV. [1] 2 4. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: min and max return single values, range returns both extremes as a pair, and which returns the positions (indices) where its logical condition is TRUE, not the values: min(x) gives [1] −1; max(x) gives [1] 10; range(x) gives [1] −1 10; which(x > 5) gives [1] 2 4. So the matching is A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV. Trap: which() gives indices; and it needs a logical argument such as x < 0. (Outputs confirmed in R 4.5.1.)

items.stem: With x <- c(−4, 7, 0, 2), match LIST-I with LIST-II. LIST-I: A. > min(x); B. > max(x); C. > range(x); D. > which(x == 0). LIST-II: I. [1] 3; II. [1] −4  7; III. [1] 7; IV. [1] −4. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: min and max return single values, range returns both extremes as a pair, and which returns the positions (indices) where its logical condition is TRUE, not the values: min(x) gives [1] −4; max(x) gives [1] 7; range(x) gives [1] −4  7; which(x == 0) gives [1] 3. So the matching is A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I. Trap: which() gives indices; and it needs a logical argument such as x < 0. (Outputs confirmed in R 4.5.1.)
